No-Code Foundations: Problems, Data and Platforms

Before you open any builder, you need to judge whether an app is the right answer, and you need to think in tables, keys and links the way every serious app does. This module gives you that judgement, the data modelling skill underneath every no-code platform, and a clear view of what the platforms cost and where the paid work is.
Spreadsheet, form, no-code app or custom code: choosing the right tool

A **no-code app builder** lets you create a working app by choosing screens, fields and rules in a visual editor instead of writing programming code. Underneath, the app still has the same three parts every app has: **data** (the information it stores), **interface** (the screens people tap and type on) and **logic** (the rules about what happens and when). The builder writes the code for you. Your job is to design those three parts well.

A **low-code** platform works the same way but also lets a developer add custom code when the visual tools run out. **Custom code** means a programmer builds everything from scratch. Custom code can do almost anything, but it costs more, takes longer and needs a developer to maintain it. No-code is fastest and cheapest, but you live inside what the platform allows.
A person assembling large building blocks
No-code means building from ready-made blocks: tables, screens and rules you configure rather than code.
Not every problem needs an app

Advanced builders are valuable because they know when **not** to build. Many problems are solved by a well-designed spreadsheet or a simple form. An app earns its place when several people must enter and see the same data, often on phones, with rules that stop mistakes. Ask these five questions before you build anything.
**How many people touch the data?** One person keeping records alone can usually stay with a spreadsheet.
**Where is the work done?** If staff work in a shop, on a farm or on the road, a phone app beats a laptop spreadsheet.
**Do records link to each other?** Customers with many orders, products with many sales: linked records are where apps shine.
**Are mistakes costly?** If a wrong price or a double booking loses money, you need rules that block bad entries.
**Does the outside public need to use it?** Public, customer-facing apps raise cost and data protection duties, so plan them carefully.

Worked example: should Nneka's tailoring workshop get an app?

For example, Nneka runs a tailoring workshop in Aba with three apprentices. Customers send styles and measurements on WhatsApp. Orders are written in a notebook, and about 60 orders a month pass through the shop. Twice last month a dress was promised for the wrong date.
People: Nneka and three apprentices all need to see orders, so four users. A private spreadsheet is not enough.
Place: the work happens at cutting tables, not at a desk, so phones matter.
Links: one customer has many orders, and each order has measurements and a due date. These are linked records.
Cost of mistakes: a missed delivery date loses a customer, so the app should show orders due in the next 3 days on its first screen.
Public use: customers do not need to log in. They keep using WhatsApp, which keeps the build internal and simpler.
An internal no-code app on AppSheet fits: four staff users, linked Customers and Orders tables, and a 'Due soon' view. A public customer app would be unnecessary cost.
Honest limits you must know
**Platform lock-in:** your app's screens and rules live on the vendor's platform. If prices rise or the product changes, moving is a rebuild, although your data in Google Sheets stays yours.
**Per-user costs:** many internal tool platforms charge per user per month, so an app for 40 staff can cost far more each year than the build fee.
**Performance:** spreadsheet-backed apps slow down as tables grow very large or formulas get heavy. Keep heavy calculations out of every row where you can.
**Complex logic:** unusual calculations, real-time features or deep integrations may need low-code or a developer.
Say it before the client asks

Professionals write the limits into the proposal: who owns the data, what the monthly platform fee is, and what would trigger a move to custom code. Clients trust a builder who names the ceiling early.

Data modelling for no-code apps: tables, keys and references
Split a business's information into separate tables, one per kind of thing
Choose a unique key for every table and explain why names make poor keys
Link tables with references for one-to-many relationships
Choose the right column types so the app can validate entries

The **data model** is the plan of what your app stores and how the pieces connect. It is the single biggest difference between an app that grows smoothly and one that becomes a mess after three months. Good no-code builders spend more time here than on screens, because screens are easy to change and data structure is not.
Linked database tables on a screen
A clean data model is a set of small tables, each about one kind of thing, linked by keys.
Rule 1: one table per kind of thing

A **table** holds one kind of thing: customers, orders, products, staff. Each **row** is one of those things and each **column** is one fact about it. In Google Sheets, each table is one tab with a single header row on top. Avoid the common beginner pattern of putting everything into one wide sheet with columns like Item1, Item2, Item3. That design breaks the day a customer brings four items.
Rule 2: every row needs a key

A **key** is a column whose value is different for every row, so the app can find exactly one record. Names make poor keys: two customers can both be called Blessing, and people change phone numbers. In AppSheet the usual practice is an ID column whose initial value is the function **UNIQUEID()**, which creates a random ID when the row is added. The user never needs to see it.
Rule 3: link tables with references

A **reference** is a column that stores the key of a row in another table. In AppSheet the column type is **Ref**. When the Orders table has a Customer column of type Ref pointing to Customers, each order belongs to one customer, and one customer can have many orders. This is a **one-to-many relationship**, the most common pattern in business apps. AppSheet then adds a related list on the customer screen so staff can see all her orders in one tap.
Laundry app data model
Customers (one)
Orders (many per customer)
Order Items (many per order)

Each arrow is a Ref column pointing back to the key of the table before it.
Worked example: modelling a laundry service

For example, Bisi runs a laundry and dry-cleaning service in Lekki. Today she writes each pickup in a book: customer name, phone, a list of clothes and a total. She wants an app her two riders and one ironing staff can use.
Tables: Customers (ID, Name, Phone, Address), Price List (ItemID, Item, Price), Orders (OrderID, Customer as Ref, Pickup Date, Status), Order Items (LineID, Order as Ref, Item as Ref, Qty).
Prices (illustrative): shirt ₦800, trousers ₦1,000, duvet ₦5,000.
An order has 4 shirts, 2 trousers and 1 duvet, entered as three Order Items rows.
Each line total is Qty times the item price: 4 × 800 = 3,200; 2 × 1,000 = 2,000; 1 × 5,000 = 5,000.
The order total adds the line totals: 3,200 + 2,000 + 5,000 = 10,200.
The order total is ₦10,200, worked out by the app from linked rows. Adding a fourth kind of item needs a new row, not a new column, so the model never breaks.

Stored columns and calculated columns

Store only facts that people enter. Values that can be worked out, such as a line total or an order total, should be calculated. In AppSheet you can add a **virtual column** with an **App formula**, for example a line total of [Qty] * [Item].[Price], where [Item].[Price] follows the reference to read the price. This is called **dereferencing**. Calculated values never disagree with the data they come from.
Price changes and old orders

If a line total always reads today's price from the Price List, raising the shirt price will silently change last month's orders. For money, copy the price into the Order Items row when the line is created (an initial value), so history stays true.

Clients rarely ask for 'an app'. They ask to stop losing stock, to know which rider delivered what, or to stop chasing members for records. Your opportunity is in those operational headaches inside businesses and organisations that are too small or too specific for packaged software, and too busy to build anything themselves.
People connected across a world map
Internal tools are cloud-based, so you can build for clients in your town or abroad.
Understand the platform bill first

Your build fee is paid once. The platform fee is paid every month, usually by the client directly. On AppSheet, building and testing is free: you can use basic app and automation features while prototyping and invite up to **10 test users** at no cost. To deploy to the whole team, the client takes a paid plan. At the time of writing, AppSheet listed **Starter**, **Core** and **Enterprise Plus** plans charged per user per month, at about US$5, US$10 and US$20 respectively, plus a per-app **Publisher Pro** option for public apps without sign-in. Prices change, so always check the official pricing page on the day you quote.
Features decide the plan
Some features need a higher plan. For example, AppSheet security filters, which limit each user to their own rows, need Core or above. List the features a client needs before you choose the plan.
Worked example: the tailoring app's running cost
For example, Nneka's tailoring app from the first lesson will have 4 users after testing. Figures use an illustrative exchange rate of ₦1,600 to US$1; use the real rate on the day.
Starter at about US$5 per user: 4 × 5 = US$20 a month, about 20 × 1,600 = ₦32,000.
Core at about US$10 per user: 4 × 10 = US$40 a month, about 40 × 1,600 = ₦64,000.
Yearly Core cost: 40 × 12 = US$480.
Nneka wants each apprentice to see only their own assigned orders, which needs security filters, so Core is the realistic plan.
Nneka should budget about US$40 a month (roughly ₦64,000 at the illustrative rate) after the free testing stage, and she should hear this before she agrees to any build fee.
Where the work is
**Cooperatives and thrift groups:** member contributions, loans and repayments that a secretary now keeps in notebooks.
**Agro-input shops and aggregators:** stock, sales and farmer records across a shop and the field.
**Service businesses:** laundries, tailoring, repairs, cleaning companies tracking jobs and staff.
**NGOs and community programmes:** field visit and beneficiary data collected offline, then synced.
**Logistics and dispatch riders:** pickups, deliveries, cash collected and proof photos.
**Remote clients abroad:** small companies that need an internal tool built on a platform they already pay for.

Value means money saved or protected, hours freed, or mistakes prevented. Effort means number of tables, users, rules and integrations. A stock tracker with three tables and five users is a quick win. A customer-facing booking app with online payments is a big project that needs careful scoping.
Foreign-currency fees: check before you promise

Most no-code platforms bill in US dollars by card. For a Nigerian client this brings two practical questions. First, can their card pay a recurring foreign subscription? Some naira cards have international spending limits or block recurring charges, so ask the client to test a payment early. Second, the naira cost moves with the exchange rate, so a fee that is affordable this year can feel heavy next year. Quote the dollar figure, show the naira estimate with the date of the rate you used, and remind the client that the vendor, not you, sets the price.

Logic is what turns a data-entry screen into a useful tool. In AppSheet, logic is written as **expressions**: short formulas, similar to spreadsheet formulas, that use column names in square brackets and functions such as SELECT, SUM, IF and TODAY. You use expressions in four main places: calculated columns, validation rules, actions and bots.
A phone showing app notifications
A bot turns data changes into alerts, so the owner hears about low stock without opening the app.
Calculating stock from linked rows

Stock is never typed in. It is calculated from the opening stock, plus everything received, minus everything sold. Add a virtual column called **Current Stock** to the Products table with this App formula:
[Opening Stock] + SUM(SELECT(Stock In[Qty], [Product] = [_THISROW].[ProductID])) - SUM(SELECT(Sales[Qty], [Product] = [_THISROW].[ProductID]))

Read it in plain words: SELECT gathers the Qty values from Stock In rows whose Product matches this product; SUM adds them; the same is done for Sales and subtracted. **[_THISROW]** means 'the product row we are calculating for'.
Worked example: NPK stock after a busy week
For example, in Esther's shop the NPK 15:15:15 product starts the month with an opening stock of 40 bags and a reorder level of 15 bags.
One delivery is recorded in Stock In: 25 bags.
Sales rows for NPK during the week add up to 52 bags.
Current Stock = 40 + 25 - 52 = 13 bags.
13 is at or below the reorder level of 15, so the product should trigger a low-stock alert.
The last sale was 3 bags at ₦38,000 (illustrative), so that sale's value is 3 × 38,000 = ₦114,000.
The app shows 13 bags left without anyone counting, and the bot you build below emails Esther that NPK needs reordering.

What it prevents

AND([_THIS] > 0, [_THIS] <= [Product].[Current Stock])

**[_THIS]** in a Valid If means 'the value being typed into this column'. **[Product].[Current Stock]** follows the Ref to the product and reads its stock. Add an error message to each Valid If, such as 'Only 13 bags left', so staff know what went wrong.
Making status visible

Numbers alone are easy to miss on a small screen. Add a second virtual column to Products called Stock Status with the formula IF([Current Stock] <= [Reorder Level], "Reorder", "OK"). Then add a **format rule** that shows Reorder in red. Sort the products deck so Reorder items appear first. Esther now sees what to buy at a glance, and the same Stock Status column can drive a 'To reorder' slice for her supplier calls.

When conditions have more than two outcomes, IFS reads more clearly than nested IFs. For example, IFS([Current Stock] <= 0, "Out", [Current Stock] <= [Reorder Level], "Reorder", TRUE, "OK") checks each condition in order and returns the first match.
Actions: one tap instead of many

An **action** is a button that does something to data. Add a Status column (Enum: Pending payment, Paid) to Sales, then create an action of type 'Data: set the values of some columns in this row' that sets Status to Paid. Add the condition [Status] = "Pending payment" so the button only appears when it makes sense. Staff now confirm a transfer with one tap instead of opening and editing the record.
Bots: automation that runs by itself

A **bot** watches for an **event**, then runs a **process** made of steps, such as sending an email or a notification. Events can be data changes (a row added, updated or deleted) or a schedule, such as every morning.

Condition: stock at reorder level
Task: email the owner
Owner reorders from supplier
The bot only fires when both the event and the condition are true.

Keep heavy formulas few

Every SELECT inside a virtual column runs across whole tables, and virtual columns are recalculated when the app syncs. On a table with thousands of rows, many such columns slow the app noticeably. Use them for the few numbers that matter, and archive old sales to a separate sheet each year.

Testing, access control, offline use and the handover pack
Write and run a test script that includes edge cases
Control who can sign in and what each role can see or change
Configure offline use and explain the risk of long offline periods
Produce a handover pack another person could maintain from

An app that works when you, the builder, use it carefully is not finished. It is finished when a busy staff member, a weak network and a careless entry cannot break it, and when someone other than you can maintain it. This lesson covers the four checks professionals do before deployment: testing, access, offline behaviour and documentation.
A person fixing bugs on a large screen
Testing means hunting for the entries that break your rules before real users find them.
Write a test script

A **test script** is a numbered list of things to try, each with the expected result. Include normal cases (a correct sale), **edge cases** (values at the limit, such as selling exactly the last bag) and wrong entries (zero, negative, blanks, duplicates). Record pass or fail for each, fix the failures and test again.
Worked example: testing Esther's app
For example, Amina is a no-code builder finishing Esther's stock and sales app. She writes 14 test cases and runs them on an Android phone signed in as a sales staff test user.
11 of 14 cases pass, so 3 fail.
Fail 1: a quantity of 0 was saved. She had written Valid If [_THIS] <= stock but forgot [_THIS] > 0, so she changes it to the AND() version.
Fail 2: two products named 'Maize seed 10kg' could be created. She adds a Valid If on Name: NOT(IN([_THIS], SELECT(Products[Name], [ProductID] <> [_THISROW].[ProductID]))).
Fail 3: a staff test user could edit the opening stock. She makes Opening Stock editable only for the owner (see roles below).
She reruns all 14 cases, not just the 3 that failed, because fixes can break other things.
All 14 cases pass on the second run. The test log, with dates and results, goes into the handover pack as proof of quality.
Control access
**Sign-in:** require users to sign in, and share the app only with the named email addresses of staff.

**Roles:** keep a small Users table (Email, Role). Use expressions such as LOOKUP(USEREMAIL(), "Users", "Email", "Role") = "Owner" in Editable If or Show If to limit who changes prices and opening stock.

**Security filters:** a Yes/No expression per table, such as [Sold By] = USEREMAIL(), that keeps rows a user should not have out of their app. They need the Core plan or above, and Google advises protecting sensitive data at the data source level too.
**The sheet itself:** anyone with edit access to the Google Sheet can change data directly. Share the sheet only with the owner and the builder.
Personal data and the law

Customer phone numbers are personal data. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 expects you to collect only what you need, tell people why, and keep it secure. Do not collect BVN, NIN or card details in a no-code app, and remove test users who have left before go-live.
Offline use

AppSheet stores the app definition and data on the phone, so staff can keep recording when the network drops. The app must first be opened while online. Edits made offline are queued and sent when the connection returns. Settings such as **Delayed sync** (queue changes until the user syncs) and **Sync on start** (force a sync when the app opens) let you balance data cost against freshness.
Long offline periods cause overwrites

Google's documentation warns that if a phone stays offline for days or weeks and then syncs, its older edits can override changes other users made in the meantime. Train field staff to sync at least daily, and design tables so each person mostly adds new rows rather than editing shared ones.

Deployment check passed

Do not move the app to a paid plan and real users until every box is ticked.
Test offline behaviour on purpose: switch a test phone to airplane mode, record two sales, reconnect, sync and confirm both rows reached the Google Sheet with the right staff email and date.

Documentation lets the client, or another builder, keep the app alive. Keep it short and practical. AppSheet's **Deployment check** in the editor flags common problems before you deploy, so run it and note the result.

Client Work: Discovery, Pricing and Your Practice

Building is half the job. This module shows you how to run a discovery session that finds the real process and its cost, how to price a build and its ongoing support without underpricing yourself, and how to turn your projects into a portfolio and a 90-day plan for paid no-code work.
Discovery: mapping the client's process and writing the app specification
Run a structured discovery conversation with a client
Map the current process step by step and measure the time it costs
Turn findings into user stories sorted as Must, Should and Could
Write a one-page app specification the client can approve

**Discovery** is the conversation and observation you do before quoting or building. Its purpose is to understand the real process, the people who do it and what it costs today. Builders who skip discovery build the app the client described, which is often not the app the client needs.
Two people in a structured conversation
Good discovery is mostly listening and watching how the work is really done.
Questions that find the real problem
Area
Question to ask
What you learn

Walk me through what happens from the moment this starts until it is finished.
The real steps, including the ones nobody wrote down

Where does it go wrong? Tell me about the last time.

A measurable goal for the proposal
Ask to **watch** the process happen once, even for 20 minutes. People describe their work as tidier than it is. What they do with a pen and a phone is the truth your app must handle.
From conversation to specification

One-page specification
Each stage feeds the next; the specification is what the client approves.
Worked example: a thrift cooperative in Owerri

For example, Ruth is the secretary of a women's thrift cooperative in Owerri with 48 members. Members contribute weekly. She records each payment in a notebook from WhatsApp transfer screenshots, then reconciles the notebook with the bank statement at month end. Times are her own estimates.
Weekly recording: about 3 minutes per member, so 48 × 3 = 144 minutes, which is 2.4 hours a week.
Monthly: 2.4 hours × 4 weeks = 9.6 hours, plus about 5 hours of month-end reconciliation, giving 14.6 hours a month.
Errors: twice in the last quarter a member was told she had not paid when she had.
Users: Ruth enters payments; the treasurer and chairperson view reports; members do not need to sign in.
Success measure agreed with Ruth: month-end reconciliation finished in under 2 hours, and no disputed payments.

The problem is about 14.6 hours of secretary time a month plus disputes that damage trust. The app is a payments register linked to a members table, with a monthly statement per member, not a members' mobile banking app.
When the client arrives with a solution

Clients often open with a solution: 'I want an app like the bank's' or 'I need a dashboard'. Do not argue and do not agree yet. Ask what that solution would let them do that they cannot do today, and keep asking until you reach a step in the process and a cost. Ruth first asked for 'an app where members log in', but the real pain was her own recording time and payment disputes, which a much smaller internal app solves.
**Red flag:** nobody can say who will enter the data every day. Apps without an owner die within weeks.
**Red flag:** the client wants every feature in version one and cannot name the most important one.
**Red flag:** sensitive data with no agreement on who may see it.
**Good sign:** one decision maker, a clear daily user and a measurable pain.
User stories and priorities

A **user story** describes one need in the form: 'As a [role], I want [action] so that [benefit].' For example: 'As the secretary, I want to record a payment by choosing a member and amount so that I stop rewriting names.' Sort stories into **Must** (the app is useless without it), **Should** (important, but can follow) and **Could** (nice to have). This is the MoSCoW method, where the W stands for 'Won't have this time'.
Must: record payments against members; show each member's total for the month; flag members who have not paid by Friday.
Should: a monthly statement each member can be sent as a PDF.
Could: a chart of total contributions per month for the annual meeting.
Won't (this time): members logging in to see their own balance.
The one-page specification

Your specification fits on one page: the problem in two sentences, the users and roles, the data model sketch, the Must and Should stories, the platform and its monthly cost, what is out of scope, and the success measure. The client signs or approves it in writing, even by WhatsApp message, before you quote a final price.
Money data needs extra care
A contributions app holds personal and financial records. Agree who may see what, keep the sheet shared only with officers, and never store members' bank login details, BVN or card numbers.

Pricing a no-code build, writing the proposal and controlling scope
Estimate a build in hours by phase and add a contingency
Separate the build fee, the platform subscription and ongoing support
Write a proposal with deliverables, exclusions and payment milestones
Handle change requests without losing money or goodwill

Underpricing is the most common mistake new builders make, because the visible part of the work, clicking in the editor, is quick. Most time goes into discovery, testing, training and fixing the things users discover. Price the whole job, and keep three costs clearly separate: your **build fee**, the client's **platform subscription** and **ongoing support**.
A signed contract document
A clear written proposal protects both you and the client when requests change.
Estimate by phase
Worked example: pricing the cooperative payments app
For example, Ruth's cooperative from the last lesson approves the specification. The builder's rate is ₦10,000 per hour, an illustrative figure; set your own from your skill and market.
Hours by phase: discovery and specification 6, data model and sheet setup 4, building views, rules and statement 16, testing 6, training and handover 4.
Total: 6 + 4 + 16 + 6 + 4 = 36 hours.
Contingency of 15% for unknowns: 360,000 × 1.15 = ₦414,000.
Milestones of 40%, 40% and 20%: ₦165,600 on approval, ₦165,600 when the test version is shown, ₦82,800 at go-live.
The proposal quotes ₦414,000 for the build in three payments that add back to ₦414,000, separate from the platform fee the cooperative pays directly.
The platform fee belongs to the client

Set up the app under an account the client owns, or plan a clear transfer, and have the client pay the platform directly. If you pay and recharge it, the app stops the day your card fails or the relationship ends. For the cooperative, three officers would use the app; at about US$5 per user on Starter that is around US$15 a month at the time of writing. State the plan, user count and that prices are set by the vendor.
Check the value before you send the quote

A client pays happily when the app clearly earns more than it costs. Do a simple **payback** check: take the monthly benefit (money saved or protected, plus staff time freed, valued honestly), subtract the monthly platform fee, and divide the build fee by what is left. The answer is the number of months before the app has paid for itself.

For example, with illustrative figures: a provision shop believes it loses about ₦50,000 a month through unrecorded sales. The platform fee is about ₦24,000 a month (US$15 at the illustrative rate of ₦1,600). The net monthly benefit is 50,000 - 24,000 = ₦26,000. A build fee of ₦300,000 pays back in 300,000 ÷ 26,000, about 11.5 months. If payback runs well beyond a year, offer a smaller first phase with only the Must stories, or fewer paid users, rather than cutting your hourly rate.
Support after go-live

Offer either a **retainer** (a fixed monthly fee for a set number of hours, such as 4 hours a month at your rate, which would be ₦40,000 at ₦10,000 per hour) or **pay-as-you-go** support at an hourly rate. Include a short free warranty period, such as 14 days, for fixing defects in what was agreed. A defect is something that does not work as specified; a new idea is a change.

Controlling scope

**Scope creep** is the slow growth of the job through small extra requests. Each one sounds tiny; together they eat your profit. Answer every request the same calm way: thank the client, check it against the specification, and if it is new, give an hour estimate and ask whether to add it now or put it in the next phase. Keep a simple change log with the date, request, hours and approval, so the final invoice has no surprises.
Payment scams target freelancers too

Never start work on a fake 'transfer alert' screenshot. Confirm the money in your own bank or Paystack, Opay or Moniepoint account before each milestone. Be wary of overpayments followed by requests to refund the difference.

Case studies, demo apps and a 90-day plan for paid no-code work
Write a short case study that shows problem, build and measured result
Prepare a safe demo app with sample data
Plan outreach in your chosen niche with weekly targets

Clients buy no-code work when they can see a working app that solves a problem like theirs. Your portfolio is therefore not a list of platforms you know. It is two or three **demo apps** they can tap through, and short **case studies** that explain the thinking and the result.
A portfolio website showing project cards
A small portfolio of real, tappable apps beats a long list of tools.
Build safe demo apps
Copy your project into a demo version filled with **made-up sample data**: invented names, numbers like 0800 000 0001 and test emails. Never show a real client's customers.
Ask permission before naming any client, and describe them generally (for example, 'a thrift cooperative in the South East') if they prefer.
Keep the demo on the free prototyping stage and share it with prospects as test users, staying within the 10-user limit.
Record your own short screen recording of the app on a phone and keep it on your portfolio page or WhatsApp catalogue.
Write case studies that persuade

A good case study is 150 to 300 words with five parts: the **client and problem**, the **old process and its cost**, **what you built** (tables, key rules, automation), the **measured result**, and a **lesson learned**. Real numbers, even small ones, convince more than adjectives. If you do not have a measurement yet, say so honestly and show the before figures.
Part
Example from the cooperative app
Problem
A secretary spent about 14.6 hours a month recording and reconciling 48 members' contributions
What was built
Members and Payments tables, an unpaid-by-Friday list, a monthly statement per member
Result
Reported by the client after two months; quote her figures only with permission
Lesson
Watching one Friday's recording session revealed that screenshots arrive in batches, so a quick-add form mattered most
Where to show your work

Keep it simple and cheap on data. A single portfolio page or a free website section with your case studies, your WhatsApp Business catalogue with one item per demo app, and a LinkedIn profile that names your niche are enough to start. Each case study should end with one clear next step, such as 'Message me for a 20-minute walkthrough of the demo'.
Outreach that respects people's time

A good first message is short and specific. Name the trade, name the problem you solve, offer something small and concrete, and make it easy to say no. For example: 'Good afternoon, Madam. I build simple phone apps for agro-input shops that show stock left without counting bags each evening. Could I show you a 10-minute demo on my phone when you are less busy this week?' Visit in person where you can; a demo on your phone at the shop counter is more convincing than any link.
Your 90-day plan
90 days to paid work
Weeks 1-4: two demo apps
Weeks 5-8: outreach and discovery
Weeks 9-12: first paid builds
Each phase produces evidence that makes the next phase easier.
Worked example: Aisha's 90-day plan

For example, Aisha, a former shop manager in Kano, chooses the niche 'stock and sales apps for agro-input and provision shops'. She has about 10 hours a week. Her targets are illustrative goals, not promised results.
Weeks 1 to 4: build two demo apps (agro-input stock and provision shop sales), about 15 hours each, which is 30 of her 40 available hours; the rest goes on case-study write-ups.
Weeks 5 to 8: list 40 shops through her market association and WhatsApp groups and contact 10 a week, so 4 × 10 = 40 contacts.
From those 40, she aims for 6 discovery conversations and 3 proposals.
Weeks 9 to 12: aim to win 1 or 2 builds, deliver the first using the full test and handover process, and ask for a testimonial at go-live.
Every Friday she records contacts made, conversations held, proposals sent and money received in a simple sheet.
By day 90 Aisha has two demos, two case studies, a tracked pipeline of 40 contacts and, if her targets hold, her first paid build. Her weekly sheet shows where to adjust.
Keep growing your skill
Work through Google's official AppSheet help centre topics on expressions, automation and security after each project.
Rebuild one demo on a second platform, such as Glide, to learn which client needs suit which tool.
Learn basic SQL and data modelling; they deepen everything you do in no-code.
Lead others: run a short demo session for your cooperative, association or WODDI circle and teach the five-question test from this course.
Charge for your second build
One free or discounted build for a case study is reasonable. After that, quote properly. Your demos and process are your proof.

Why this matters
Every app has three parts
Data: the information it stores
Interface: the screens people use
Logic: the rules about what happens
A no-code app builder lets you create a working app by choosing screens, fields and rules, instead of writing code. Underneath, every app has three parts. Data, the information it stores.
Interface, the screens people tap and type on.
And logic, the rules about what happens and when. The builder writes the code. Your job is to design these three parts well.
Before you build
Five questions: does it need an app?
How many people touch the data?
Where is the work done?
Do records link to each other?
Are mistakes costly?
Does the public need to use it?
Good builders know when not to build. Use the simplest tool that works: spreadsheet, then form, then no-code app, then custom code.
For example, Nneka runs a tailoring workshop in Aba with three apprentices. Four people need to see orders, so a private spreadsheet is not enough.
The work happens at cutting tables, not a desk, so phones matter.
One customer has many orders. Those are linked records, where apps shine.
Twice last month a dress was promised for the wrong date. So the first screen should show orders due in the next 3 days.
Customers keep using WhatsApp, so the app stays internal and simpler. An internal app on Google AppSheet fits.

Four rules for your data model

One table per kind of thing

Link tables with Ref columns
Pick the right column type
The data model is the plan of what your app stores and how the pieces connect. Screens are easy to change. Data structure is not.
Rule one: one table per kind of thing. Avoid columns like Item1, Item2, Item3. That breaks the day a customer brings four items.
Rule two: every row needs a key, a value different for every row. Names make poor keys, because two customers can both be called Blessing.
Rule three: a Ref column stores the key of a row in another table. One customer, many orders. That is a one-to-many link.
Rule four: choose column types like Date, Enum or Phone. They give you free checking and the right keyboard.
Worked example
Bisi's laundry order, worked out by the app
For example, Bisi runs a laundry and dry-cleaning service in Lekki.
4 shirts at 800
2 trousers at 1,000
1 duvet at 5,000
Illustrative naira prices.
Bisi has four tables: Customers, Price List, Orders and Order Items. Each order item is one row, linked to its order and its item.
Each line total is quantity times price. 4 shirts make 3,200 naira. 2 trousers make 2,000. 1 duvet is 5,000.
The order total is 10,200 naira, calculated by the app. Adding a new kind of item needs a new row, not a new column.
One warning. For money, copy the price into the order line when it is created. Otherwise raising the shirt price silently changes last month's orders.
Honest limits
Name the ceiling before you build
Screens and rules live on the vendor's platform. Moving is a rebuild, though your data in Sheets stays yours.
Many platforms charge per user per month. An app for 40 staff can cost more each year than the build fee.
Spreadsheet-backed apps slow down as tables grow very large or formulas get heavy.
Professionals tell the client the limits early. First, lock-in. If prices rise, moving is a rebuild.
Second, per-user cost, which can be bigger than your build fee.
Third, performance slows as tables grow very large.
Platform bill
Nneka's monthly AppSheet cost
For example, Nneka's app has 4 users, at an illustrative rate of 1,600 naira to US$1.
Starter: 4 users at US$5
Core: 4 users at US$10
Illustrative rate. Check today's prices.
Your build fee is paid once. The platform fee is paid every month, usually by the client. AppSheet is free while you prototype, with up to 10 test users. To deploy, the client needs a paid plan.
On Starter, at about US$5 per user, Nneka would pay US$20 a month, about 32,000 naira.

She wants each apprentice to see only their own orders. That needs security filters, which need Core. So she budgets about US$40 a month, roughly 64,000 naira. She should hear this before she agrees to any build fee.
Opportunities
Where the paid work is
Cooperatives and thrift groups
Agro-input shops and aggregators
Laundries, tailoring, repairs, cleaning
NGOs and field programmes
Dispatch riders and logistics
Clients rarely ask for an app. They ask to stop losing stock, or to know which rider delivered what. Choose a niche, a client type plus an app type, so your second build reuses your first.
Start with quick wins: high value, low effort, like a stock tracker with three tables.
Protect your client
Before you quote
Check today's official pricing page
Can their card pay a US dollar subscription?
Show naira estimate with the rate's date
Collect only the data that is needed
Before you quote, check the official pricing page that day. Some naira cards block recurring foreign charges, so ask the client to test a payment early.
And clinics, lenders and savings groups hold sensitive data. Under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, collect only what is needed and keep it secure. Start with stock, jobs and logistics apps.
Key points
Remember
Use the simplest tool that works
One table per kind of thing, with a key
Ref columns link one to many
Platform fees are monthly and per user
Name the limits before you build
To remember. Use the simplest tool that works. Give every table a key and link with references. Budget monthly per-user fees. And name the limits before you build.

Module 2 video
Build, test and hand over a stock and sales app
Build, test and hand over a stock and sales app.
This is the video for module two of No-Code App Development.
What you will build
Esther's agro-input shop app
Track products, deliveries and sales
Warn the owner when stock runs low
Tested, secured and documented
In this module you build one real app. For example, Esther runs an agro-input shop in Makurdi, with two sales staff. She wants to stop counting bags every evening.
Her app will track products, deliveries and sales, warn her when stock is low, and be tested and documented so someone else can run it. It all works on AppSheet's free prototyping stage.
Step 1
Prepare the sheet properly
One table per tab: Products, Stock In, Sales
Exactly one header row in row 1
No merged cells, totals rows or blank rows
An ID column first in every tab
3 to 5 realistic sample rows
Most early problems come from messy sheets. AppSheet reads each tab as a table, with one header row on top.
Remove merged cells and totals rows. Esther deleted a TOTAL row at the bottom of her Sales tab, because AppSheet would read it as a sale.
Put an ID column first, and add a few sample rows so AppSheet can guess column types.
Step by step
Never accept AppSheet's column guesses blindly.
After the sheet, check every column. Keys get the initial value UNIQUEID(), and are hidden. Dates start as TODAY(). Sold By records USEREMAIL().
The Product column in Sales and Stock In becomes a Ref to Products, linking every sale to one product.
Design views for staff at a counter with a phone in one hand. New sale goes first in the menu, because it is the most frequent task.
Follow this order. Changing the data after views are built causes rework. And test on a real phone, not only in the editor.
Logic
Stock is calculated, never typed
13 is at or below the reorder level of 15: time to reorder.
Opening stock: 40 bags of NPK
Plus deliveries: 25 bags
Minus sales this week: 52 bags
Current Stock: 40 + 25 - 52 = 13
Logic is written as expressions, short formulas with column names in square brackets. Add a virtual column called Current Stock. NPK starts the month with 40 bags.
SELECT and SUM add every delivery for this product: 25 bags.
Then subtract every sale: 52 bags.
The app shows 13 bags left without anyone counting. With a reorder level of 15, NPK shows Reorder in red.
Stop bad data at entry
Qty and Product must be filled, so no sale is saved without them.
Qty above 0 and no more than Current Stock. Add a clear error message.
Unit Price copies the product price at the time of sale. No retyping.
Make Qty and Product required.
Add a Valid If, so quantity must be above 0 and no more than the stock. Add a message like, only 13 bags left, so staff know what went wrong.
And copy the price into the sale when it is made, so history stays true.
Automation
A low-stock bot
A bot fires only when the event and condition are both true.
Condition: stock at or below reorder level
Test until the email arrives
A bot watches for an event, then runs steps by itself. Here the event is a new row in Sales.
The condition checks the product's stock against its reorder level. If true, it emails Esther the product name and stock.
Record test sales until the condition is met, and confirm the email arrives. Keep heavy formulas few, because they slow the app as tables grow.
Testing
Amina's test script
After any fix, rerun every case, not just the failures.
Write 14 cases with expected results
Include edge cases and wrong entries
11 of 14 pass; fix the 3 failures
Rerun all 14 cases
For example, Amina is finishing Esther's app. She writes 14 test cases, including selling exactly the last bag, and entering zero or blanks. She runs them as a sales staff test user.
3 fail. A quantity of 0 was saved, two products could share a name, and staff could edit the opening stock. She fixes each one.
Then she reruns all 14, because fixes can break other things. All pass, and the test log goes into the handover pack.
Safety first
Access, data and offline use
Share with named staff emails. Only the owner changes prices and stock. Limit who edits the sheet.
Collect only what you need. Never collect BVN, NIN or card details in a no-code app.
Days offline can overwrite others' changes. Staff sync at least daily.
Require sign-in, and use a Users table with roles so only the owner changes prices. Anyone with edit access to the Google Sheet can change data, so share it only with the owner and builder.
Customer phone numbers are personal data. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 expects you to collect only what you need and keep it secure.
AppSheet works offline, but a phone offline for days can overwrite other people's changes when it syncs. Test it in airplane mode.
Key points
Remember
Clean sheets first; check every column
Calculate stock from linked rows
Valid If and Required stop bad entries
Rerun every test after a fix
Handover pack: model, rules, users, costs, tests

To remember. Clean the sheet and check every column. Calculate stock, never type it. Block bad entries. Rerun all tests after fixes. And deliver a handover pack, so someone other than you can keep the app alive.

Discovery, pricing and your first paid no-code clients
Discovery, pricing, and your first paid no-code clients.
This is the video for module three of No-Code App Development.
Why this matters
Building is half the job
Find the real process and its cost
Price the whole job, not just clicking
Turn projects into paid work
Builders who skip discovery build the app the client described, which is often not the app the client needs.
In this video you will learn to find the real problem, price your work without underpricing yourself, and plan your first 90 days of paid work.
Discovery
Six questions that find the real problem
Walk me through what happens, start to finish
Where does it go wrong? The last time?
How long does each step take, how often?
Who enters data, who reads it, what phones?
Can I see the notebook or sheet you use now?
In three months, how will you know it worked?
Discovery is the conversation and observation you do before quoting. Ask for the real steps, and for the last time it went wrong.
Measure time, and find out who uses the data and on what phones.
Ask to see the real notebook, and agree a success measure. Then watch the process happen once, even for 20 minutes. People describe their work as tidier than it is.
Worked example
What Ruth's process costs today
Measure hours and errors now, so you can show the improvement later.
48 members x 3 minutes = 144 minutes a week
2.4 hours x 4 weeks = 9.6 hours
Plus 5 hours reconciliation = 14.6 hours
Twice last quarter: a paid member told she owed
For example, Ruth is secretary of a thrift cooperative in Owerri with 48 members. She records each weekly payment from transfer screenshots, about 3 minutes per member.
That is 2.4 hours a week, and with month-end reconciliation, 14.6 hours a month.

And twice last quarter, a member was wrongly told she had not paid. Ruth first asked for an app where members log in. But the real pain was her own time and the disputes, which a much smaller internal app solves.
Keep version one small
Sort user stories with MoSCoW
Must: record payments, flag unpaid by Friday
Should: monthly statement as a PDF
Could: a contributions chart
Won't this time: member log-in
Write each need as a user story: as the secretary, I want to record a payment by choosing a member, so I stop rewriting names. Must stories make the app useful at all.
Should and Could stories can follow. Won't means not this time. Put it all on a one-page specification, and get the client's approval in writing, even by WhatsApp, before you quote a final price.
Pricing
Pricing the cooperative app
For example, 36 hours at an illustrative 10,000 naira an hour, plus 15% contingency.
Spec approved: 40%
Test version shown: 40%
Go-live: 20%
Illustrative naira figures. Set your own rate.
Underpricing is the most common mistake, because clicking in the editor is quick. Estimate every phase: discovery 6 hours, setup 4, building 16, testing 6, and training 4. That is 36 hours.
At 10,000 naira an hour, that is 360,000 naira. Add 15 percent for unknowns.
Tie each payment to something the client can see. 40 percent when the specification is approved, 40 percent when the test version is shown, and 20 percent at go-live.
The build fee is 414,000 naira, and the three payments add back to that total.
Keep them separate
Three different costs
Paid to you once, in milestones, for discovery, building, testing and training.
The client pays the vendor directly, under an account the client owns.
A monthly retainer or hourly support, after a short free warranty such as 14 days.
Keep three costs clearly separate. Your build fee.
The platform fee, which the client pays directly. For three officers on Starter, about US$15 a month. If you pay it for them, the app stops the day your card fails.
And support. For example, a retainer of 4 hours a month, which is 40,000 naira at 10,000 an hour. A defect is something that does not work as specified. A new idea is a change.
Scope
Handle extra requests calmly
New requests are estimated in hours and approved in writing.
Thank the client
Check it against the specification
If new, give an hour estimate
Ask: add it now, or next phase?
Record it in your change log
Scope creep is the slow growth of the job through small extra requests. Each sounds tiny. Together they eat your profit. First, thank the client and check the specification.
If it is new, estimate the hours and ask whether to add it now or later. Log the date, request, hours and approval, so the final invoice has no surprises.
Safety first
Protect money and data
Never start work on a screenshot. Confirm the money in your own account first.
Be wary of overpayments followed by requests to refund the difference.
Share the sheet only with officers. Never store bank logins, BVN or card numbers.
Payment scams target freelancers too. Never start work on a transfer alert screenshot. Confirm the money in your own account before each milestone.
Be wary of overpayments followed by a request to refund the difference.
And a contributions app holds personal and financial records. Agree who may see what, and never store bank logins, BVN or card numbers.
Your 90 days
Aisha's plan for paid work
Weeks 1-4: build two demo apps
Weeks 5-8: contact 40 shops, 10 a week
Aim for 6 conversations and 3 proposals
Weeks 9-12: win and deliver first builds
For example, Aisha in Kano chooses stock and sales apps for shops. She builds two demo apps with made-up sample data. Never show a real client's customers.
Then she contacts 40 shops through her market association, aiming for 6 discovery conversations and 3 proposals.
By weeks 9 to 12 she aims for her first paid build, and asks for a testimonial at go-live. Every Friday she records contacts, proposals and money received.
Key points
Remember
Watch the work and measure its cost
Keep version one to the Must stories
Estimate every phase and add contingency
Separate build fee, platform fee and support
Confirm payment in your own account
To remember. Watch the work and measure what it costs. Keep version one small. Price every phase. Keep the three costs separate. And always confirm payment in your own account.
